name: TileDB
vendor: TileDB, Inc. (trading as Tile.ai since September 2026)
license: MIT for the engine (TileDB Embedded), its language APIs and the published format specification; the company’s hosted platform and its new Tile.ai product are commercial
summary: An embeddable C++ storage engine and open format for dense and sparse multi-dimensional arrays, on local disk or cloud object storage.
intro: TileDB stores data as multi-dimensional arrays. A dense array fills every cell of a grid, like an image or a climate model’s lattice. A sparse array stores only the cells that exist, keyed by their coordinates, like genomic variants by sample and position or the points of a LiDAR scan. Dataframes and key-value data are stored as sparse arrays too; TileDB 2.0 (2020) added string dimensions and dimensions of different types for that. Cells are grouped into fixed-size tiles, each attribute is stored in its own files and run through a chain of compression, encryption and checksum filters, so a read fetches only the tiles and attributes a slice touches.

Every write creates an immutable fragment: a folder of files whose name carries the time range it covers, in milliseconds. Old files are never edited, which turns random writes into sequential ones and suits object stores such as S3, Google Cloud Storage and Azure Blob Storage. Readers merge fragments, with the newest value winning, and can open the array as of an earlier timestamp. As fragments pile up, consolidation merges them and vacuuming removes the ones it replaced. The engine is a C++ library with C, C++, Python, R, Java, Go and C# APIs, and domain packages build on it: TileDB-VCF for genomic variants, TileDB-SOMA for single-cell data and TileDB-Vector-Search.

TileDB, Inc. built a commercial platform around the engine. In September 2026 the company renamed itself Tile.ai and pivoted to a governed data layer for AI agents, then in private preview. Its founder wrote that the open-source engine “will keep going, under the TileDB name, exactly as it is.”
strengths: One engine for dense and sparse data of any dimensionality, from images and genomes to dataframes
Built for object storage: immutable fragments, parallel I/O and a multi-threaded C++ core
Versioning built in: open an array as of any earlier timestamp
MIT licence and a published, versioned format specification
limits: A library you embed, not a database server; sharing and governance were the job of the company’s commercial platform
Many small writes mean many fragments, and reads slow down until you consolidate and vacuum
Its own format: other tools need a TileDB library or integration to read the data
The company’s focus moved to Tile.ai in 2026; the engine is still maintained, but check release activity before betting on it

with tiledb.open(uri, timestamp=ts_ms) as A:  # the array as it was at ts_ms

story: TileDB began as research at Intel Labs and MIT. Scientific data such as genomes, images and sensor grids are naturally arrays, but the standard array library, HDF5, handled sparse arrays poorly and was slow at small, scattered in-place writes. A 2016 paper by Stavros Papadopoulos, Kushal Datta, Samuel Madden and Timothy Mattson described a storage manager built for both dense and sparse arrays, with writes grouped into fragments. It reported HDF5-level speed on dense arrays, much faster random writes, and big wins over the SciDB array database; the Broad Institute was already using it for terabytes of genomic data.

TileDB, Inc. spun out of MIT and Intel in 2017 with a $1 million round co-led by Nexus and Intel Capital, and released TileDB 1.0 that October, a substantial rewrite of the earlier Intel code. A $4 million round followed in January 2019 and a $15 million series A, led by Two Bear Capital, in 2020. TileDB 2.0 (April 2020) brought string and mixed-type dimensions, which let dataframes live in sparse arrays, and native Google Cloud Storage and Azure Blob Storage support. The company sold a hosted platform for genomics, single-cell, imaging and geospatial work.

On September 16, 2026 the company announced it was becoming Tile.ai, a product that leaves data where it lives and exposes it to AI agents under each user’s identity. Papadopoulos stepped back from CEO to focus on product, George Llado became CEO, and Amgen and Two Bear Capital backed the change. The open-source engine keeps the TileDB name.

choices.choice: Everything is an array, dense or sparse
choices.why: Each scientific field had built its own incompatible tools, and HDF5 captured sparse data badly. The bet was that one engine handling both kinds of array could replace many silos.

Writing each batch as a new fragment turns random writes into sequential ones and avoids slow small in-place updates. The timestamps also give versioning and time travel; consolidation merges fragments later, in the background.

Papadopoulos described it in 2020 as a database focused on “universal storage and data management rather than the compute layer, which we have instead made ‘pluggable’”, so Spark, Dask, GDAL or Python could sit on top.
The founder later called it a choice for an open format, “published and unencumbered, rather than a proprietary black box”; the spec lives in the repository next to the code.
